Separate jugs let the machine skip proportioning with treated water

explanation: Acid concentrate contains sodium chloride, potassium, calcium, magnesium, a small amount of acid and often dextrose. Stored with bicarbonate, calcium and magnesium would precipitate as carbonate salts, so the machine proportions the two concentrates with treated water only at the point of use.

distractorExplanations.a: Dextrose is not neutralized by bicarbonate; the chemical problem with premixing is calcium and magnesium carbonate precipitation.
distractorExplanations.c: Potassium content is fixed by the acid concentrate chosen; premixing the two concentrates does not raise it.
distractorExplanations.d: The machine still proportions both concentrates with treated water; keeping them separate exists to prevent precipitation.

prompt: A patient taking digoxin is prescribed a higher-potassium dialysate bath, but the station is set up with a 1 mEq/L potassium bath. Why does this matter?

options.text: A low-potassium bath slows urea clearance and reduces Kt/V
A low-potassium bath raises serum calcium and causes cramps
A low-potassium bath increases fluid removal and causes hypotension
A rapid potassium drop raises the risk of dangerous arrhythmias

explanation: Potassium moves from blood to dialysate along its concentration gradient, so a lower bath removes potassium faster. Rapid falls in serum potassium, especially in patients on digoxin, can trigger arrhythmias; the bath must match the prescription, and a mismatch is corrected before starting.

distractorExplanations.a: The potassium bath does not change urea clearance; urea removal depends on the dialyzer, blood and dialysate flows, and time.
distractorExplanations.b: Bath potassium does not raise calcium; the danger of a low bath is a rapid serum potassium drop and arrhythmia.
distractorExplanations.c: Fluid removal is set by the UF goal, not by bath potassium; the concern here is heart rhythm, not blood pressure.

prompt: A prescription says to stop the heparin pump before the end of treatment. What is the purpose of stopping it early?

options.text: To let clotting recover so needle sites seal after removal
To prevent heparin from entering the dialysate during rinseback
To lower the chance of air entering the line from the syringe
To allow the dialyzer to clot slightly so it can be reused

explanation: Systemic heparin keeps the extracorporeal circuit from clotting, but its effect persists after treatment. Stopping the heparin pump at the time set in the prescription (often 30–60 minutes before the end) lets clotting begin to recover and reduces prolonged bleeding from needle sites.

distractorExplanations.b: Heparin stays in the blood compartment; rinseback returns blood with saline and does not push heparin into the dialysate.
distractorExplanations.c: Air risk from the heparin line is managed by secure connections, not by the timing of the heparin stop.
distractorExplanations.d: Deliberate clotting would ruin a reused dialyzer; reuse requires an open fiber bundle that passes volume testing.

prompt: During a saline flush, the technician sees dark streaks in the dialyzer fibers and clots in the venous drip chamber. What do these findings indicate?

options.text: Hemolysis caused by overheated or hypotonic dialysate
Clotting in the blood circuit and the dialyzer fibers
A ruptured membrane letting dialysate into the blood
Normal deposits that do not affect treatment delivery

explanation: Dark streaks or dark fibers in the dialyzer, clots in the drip chamber, and rising venous or pre-dialyzer pressures are signs of circuit clotting. Clotting reduces clearance and can cause blood loss, so the technician reports it and follows protocol for anticoagulation review or a circuit change.

distractorExplanations.a: Hemolysis turns venous blood cherry-red or translucent; it does not create dark streaked fibers and drip-chamber clots.
distractorExplanations.c: A ruptured membrane triggers the blood leak alarm with pink dialysate, not dark streaks in the fibers.
distractorExplanations.d: Visible clotting reduces the working membrane surface and clearance; it is not a normal finding to ignore.

prompt: On a modern volumetric dialysis machine, how is the exact amount of fluid removed from the patient controlled?

options.text: By raising venous pressure until the TMP reaches the goal
By adjusting dialysate sodium to pull water osmotically
By slowing the blood pump in proportion to the UF goal
By balancing chambers plus a UF pump set to the goal

explanation: Volumetric machines use balancing chambers so the dialysate volume entering and leaving the dialyzer is equal, then a separate UF pump removes exactly the programmed volume. This is essential with high-flux dialyzers, whose high water permeability makes pressure-based UF control unsafe.

distractorExplanations.a: Manually raising venous pressure was an old pressure-control method; volumetric machines measure volumes directly instead.
distractorExplanations.b: Dialysate sodium affects plasma sodium and vascular refill, but it is not the mechanism that sets the UF volume.
distractorExplanations.c: Blood flow affects clearance; on volumetric machines fluid removal is set by the UF pump, independent of pump speed.

prompt: Why are the dialyzer and bloodlines primed with normal saline before the patient is connected?

options.text: To pre-load the circuit with heparin and prevent clotting
To warm the dialyzer to body temperature before use
To remove air and rinse out residual sterilant or debris
To test whether the dialysate conductivity is in range

explanation: Priming fills the blood compartment with saline, pushing out air and rinsing away manufacturing residues or sterilant (for reused dialyzers, the germicide) before blood enters. A poorly primed circuit risks air reaching the patient and reactions to residual chemicals.

distractorExplanations.a: Heparin is given per order through the heparin line or as a bolus; priming saline is not the anticoagulation step.
distractorExplanations.b: Dialysate temperature is controlled by the machine heater; priming is about removing air and residue.
distractorExplanations.d: Conductivity is a dialysate-side check done by the machine; saline priming fills the blood side of the circuit.

prompt: The arterial and venous bloodlines were accidentally connected to the wrong needles (reversed). What is the main effect on treatment?

options.text: Venous pressure falls and the air detector is bypassed
Access recirculation rises, lowering the delivered dose
Ultrafiltration doubles because blood passes twice
Blood flow stops because the pump runs against the access

explanation: With reversed lines, cleaned blood returned upstream is drawn straight back into the arterial needle, so access recirculation rises substantially and the delivered dialysis dose falls. Lines are reversed only on order when inflow is poor; otherwise correct placement is checked at every start.

distractorExplanations.a: Line reversal does not bypass the venous air detector, which stays on the return line; the problem is recirculation.
distractorExplanations.c: UF is set by the machine's UF control and is not doubled by blood that recirculates through the access.
distractorExplanations.d: The pump still runs and blood still flows; the issue is that treated blood is redrawn, not that flow stops.

prompt: A prescription calls for sodium modeling: dialysate sodium starts higher and is lowered during treatment. What is the intended benefit, and what is the main downside?

options.text: Better refill and fewer cramps, but more thirst and weight gain
Faster urea clearance early on, with risk of disequilibrium near the end
Lower potassium at the start, with risk of arrhythmia during the session
Less heparin needed, with risk of clotting as the sodium level drops

explanation: Higher early dialysate sodium raises plasma osmolality, helping fluid move from tissues into the blood so UF is tolerated with fewer cramps and less hypotension. The trade-off is net sodium gain, which can cause post-dialysis thirst, larger interdialytic weight gains and higher blood pressure.

distractorExplanations.b: Sodium modeling does not speed urea clearance; higher sodium is actually used to reduce disequilibrium symptoms.
distractorExplanations.c: Sodium profiling changes sodium, not potassium; potassium is set by the acid concentrate bath that is prescribed.
distractorExplanations.d: Dialysate sodium has no anticoagulant effect, so it does not change heparin needs or the risk of clotting.

prompt: A dialyzer has an ultrafiltration coefficient (KUf) of 10 mL/hr/mmHg and runs at a transmembrane pressure of 100 mmHg. About how much fluid will it remove per hour?

options.text: 10 mL/hr
100 mL/hr
110 mL/hr
1,000 mL/hr

explanation: KUf is the volume of plasma water the dialyzer removes per hour for each mmHg of TMP. UF rate ≈ KUf × TMP = 10 mL/hr/mmHg × 100 mmHg = 1,000 mL/hr. This is why dialyzers with a high KUf need volumetric UF control: a small pressure change moves a lot of fluid.

distractorExplanations.a: 10 mL/hr is just the KUf value, which is per mmHg; it must be multiplied by the 100 mmHg TMP.
distractorExplanations.b: 100 mL/hr is the TMP number with mL/hr attached; the coefficient of 10 still has to multiply it.
distractorExplanations.c: 110 mL/hr adds the two figures together; KUf and TMP are multiplied, not added.

prompt: Arterial pressure has been steady at −180 mmHg; it suddenly moves toward zero and bubbles appear in the arterial line before the pump. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The venous needle has infiltrated, raising pressure in the return line
The dialyzer is clotting and resistance after the pump has increased
A leak or separation in the arterial segment is drawing in air
The patient's blood pressure has risen and access inflow has improved

explanation: The pre-pump arterial segment is under negative pressure, so a loose connection or crack there sucks air in and the reading moves toward zero. Air drawn into the blood path is dangerous: stop the pump, clamp, find and fix the leak, and clear air per protocol before resuming.

distractorExplanations.a: Venous infiltration raises venous (post-dialyzer) pressure; it does not pull bubbles into the pre-pump arterial line.
distractorExplanations.b: Dialyzer clotting raises pre-dialyzer pressure after the pump; it does not bring arterial pressure to zero with bubbles.
distractorExplanations.d: Better inflow could make arterial pressure less negative, but it would not introduce air bubbles into the line.

prompt: A patient asks how peritoneal dialysis (PD) differs from in-center hemodialysis. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: PD filters blood through an external dialyzer at home overnight
PD removes fluid by pressure from a pump, like hemodialysis UF
PD requires an AV fistula, but uses a smaller needle than hemodialysis
PD uses the peritoneal membrane in the abdomen as the dialyzer

explanation: In PD, dialysate is instilled through a peritoneal catheter and the peritoneal membrane acts as the dialyzer. Solutes move by diffusion and fluid is removed by osmosis driven by dextrose (or icodextrin) in the solution; no blood leaves the body and no vascular access is needed.

distractorExplanations.a: An external dialyzer filtering blood describes home hemodialysis, not PD, where blood never leaves the body.
distractorExplanations.b: PD fluid removal is osmotic, driven by dextrose or icodextrin in the solution, not by a hydrostatic pump gradient.
distractorExplanations.c: PD uses a catheter into the peritoneal cavity; it needs no fistula and no needles.

prompt: Mid-treatment a patient's blood pressure drops and they feel lightheaded and nauseated. Following typical standing orders, what should the technician do first?

options.text: Raise the UF rate so the goal is reached before the pressure falls further
Sit the patient fully upright and give oral fluids, then recheck in an hour
Disconnect the patient at once and send them to the waiting room to rest
Lower the head, pause UF, give saline per order, and notify the RN

explanation: Symptomatic hypotension is usually managed by placing the patient with head lowered or legs raised, reducing or pausing ultrafiltration, and giving a saline bolus per standing order, then notifying the nurse and rechecking blood pressure. Exact steps follow facility protocol.

distractorExplanations.a: Increasing UF removes fluid faster and worsens hypotension; UF is reduced or paused first.
distractorExplanations.b: Sitting upright lowers blood flow to the brain further, and waiting an hour delays treatment of a falling pressure.
distractorExplanations.c: Disconnecting an unstable patient and leaving them unmonitored risks fainting and falls; stabilize at the chair first.

prompt: A patient who missed their last treatment arrives with muscle weakness and an irregular pulse. Which problem should the technician report to the nurse immediately?

options.text: Possible hyperkalemia, which can cause fatal arrhythmias
Possible hypokalemia from potassium lost in the missed session
Possible hypercalcemia from vitamin D taken between sessions
Possible anemia from a reduced erythropoietin dose

explanation: Potassium accumulates between treatments, and a missed session can push it to dangerous levels. Weakness, tingling and an irregular pulse suggest hyperkalemia, which can cause cardiac arrest, so the nurse is told at once and urgent labs or an ECG are obtained per order.

distractorExplanations.b: A missed session means potassium was not removed, so it rises; low potassium is the opposite of what is expected.
distractorExplanations.c: Hypercalcemia causes fatigue and confusion but is not the expected emergency after a missed session; potassium is.
distractorExplanations.d: Anemia develops over weeks and causes fatigue, not acute weakness with an irregular pulse after one missed treatment.

prompt: Which type of vascular access generally has the lowest infection risk and the longest patency for long-term hemodialysis?

options.text: Tunneled central venous catheter
Synthetic AV graft
Native arteriovenous fistula
Non-tunneled femoral catheter

explanation: A native AV fistula uses the patient's own artery and vein, so once mature it has the lowest rates of infection and clotting and the longest survival. Grafts are the second choice, and catheters carry the highest bloodstream-infection risk, which drives national “fistula first, catheter last” efforts.

distractorExplanations.a: Tunneled catheters carry the highest bloodstream-infection risk of long-term accesses and are a last resort.
distractorExplanations.b: Grafts can be used sooner but clot and become infected more often than fistulas, with shorter patency.
distractorExplanations.d: Non-tunneled femoral catheters are short-term emergency access with a high infection risk.

prompt: A lab worker wants to draw blood and place a blood pressure cuff on a patient's fistula arm between treatments. What should the dialysis technician advise?

options.text: Allow it if the fistula is more than six months old
Use the other arm to protect the access from injury
Allow the cuff but draw the blood from the fistula site
Allow it if pressure is held on the site afterward

explanation: The access arm is protected: no blood pressure cuffs, IVs or routine venipuncture, and no tight clothing, jewelry or sleeping on it. Compression and extra punctures can damage the vessel and cause clotting or stenosis, so the other arm or another site is used.

distractorExplanations.a: Fistula age does not make cuffs or punctures safe; mature accesses still clot from compression and injury.
distractorExplanations.c: A blood pressure cuff compresses the access and can cause thrombosis; extra punctures outside dialysis also damage it.
distractorExplanations.d: Holding pressure afterward does not undo cuff compression or the vessel damage caused by extra punctures.

prompt: When cannulating an AV fistula, which direction should the venous (return) needle point?

options.text: Toward the hand, against the flow of blood in the access
Toward the anastomosis, so it sits close to the arterial needle
Perpendicular to the vessel, so the tip rests in the center
Toward the heart, in the same direction as access blood flow

explanation: Returned blood must travel with access flow toward the heart, so the venous needle is placed antegrade (pointing toward the heart) and downstream of the arterial needle. Pointing it against flow increases turbulence and venous pressure; the arterial needle may face either way per facility policy.

distractorExplanations.a: Pointing against flow sends returned blood into oncoming access flow and raises pressure; that is an option only for the arterial needle.
distractorExplanations.b: Placing the venous needle close to and toward the arterial needle promotes recirculation of cleaned blood.
distractorExplanations.c: Needles are inserted at an angle and advanced along the vessel; a perpendicular needle risks puncturing the back wall.

prompt: A patient uses the buttonhole cannulation technique. Which statement describes it correctly?

options.text: Sharp needles are used at new sites each treatment, rotating along the vessel
The scab is left in place and the needle is pushed through it to limit bleeding
After a track forms, blunt needles enter the same sites at the same angle
It is used mainly in grafts, where the material forms a lasting tunnel

explanation: Buttonhole cannulation uses the exact same sites and angle until a scar tunnel forms, after which blunt needles are used. Scabs are removed aseptically and the site cleaned before each cannulation because buttonholes carry a higher infection risk than rope-ladder rotation.

distractorExplanations.a: Rotating sharp needles along the vessel is the rope-ladder technique, the opposite of buttonhole cannulation.
distractorExplanations.b: Pushing a needle through a scab carries skin bacteria into the track; scabs are removed aseptically first.
distractorExplanations.d: Buttonholes are created in native fistulas; synthetic graft material does not form a stable tunnel and is not used this way.

prompt: After needle removal, how should pressure be held on a fistula site to stop bleeding safely?

options.text: Firmly enough to stop the thrill completely for at least 20 minutes
Gently over the puncture site, with the thrill still felt nearby
With a tight tape-and-gauze wrap that stays on until the next session
By pressing hard before the needle is fully out, to prevent a bleed

explanation: Hemostasis needs enough gentle pressure to seal the puncture while blood still flows through the access, confirmed by a palpable thrill or audible bruit. Occluding the access can make it clot; bleeding that lasts longer than usual is reported because it can signal stenosis or excess heparin.

distractorExplanations.a: Stopping the thrill means the access is occluded, which can cause thrombosis; pressure should not cut off flow.
distractorExplanations.c: Tight wraps left on for hours compress the access and risk clotting; dressings are checked and removed per policy.
distractorExplanations.d: Pressing before the needle is fully out drags the bevel against the vessel and can tear it; press after removal.

prompt: A patient's target weight is 70.0 kg and pre-dialysis weight is 73.2 kg. The unit adds 0.3 L for rinseback and fluids taken during treatment. What UF goal should be programmed?
explanation: Interdialytic gain = 73.2 − 70.0 = 3.2 kg, which is about 3.2 L of fluid. Fluid given during treatment must also be removed, so UF goal = 3.2 + 0.3 = 3.5 L. Units differ in what they add, so follow the facility's UF-goal policy and the prescription.

distractorExplanations.a: 2.9 L subtracts the 0.3 L instead of adding it; rinseback and intake add fluid that must also be removed.
distractorExplanations.b: 3.2 L is the weight gain alone; it leaves out the 0.3 L the patient will receive during treatment.
distractorExplanations.d: 3.8 L adds the 0.3 L twice; the correct goal is the 3.2 L gain plus 0.3 L, or 3.5 L.

prompt: A patient with a tunneled catheter develops shaking chills and a fever soon after the catheter lines are connected. Which problem should be suspected first?

options.text: A catheter-related bloodstream infection
A first-use reaction to the dialyzer membrane
Disequilibrium from rapid urea removal
Hypotension from too high an ultrafiltration rate

explanation: Rigors and fever that start soon after a catheter is flushed or connected are a classic sign of catheter-related bloodstream infection, because bacteria in the lumen are pushed into the blood. Notify the nurse at once; blood cultures and antibiotics are ordered by the provider.

distractorExplanations.b: First-use reactions cause chest or back pain and itching in the first minutes, not fever with rigors linked to catheter use.
distractorExplanations.c: Disequilibrium causes headache, nausea and confusion, mainly in early treatments, not fever and shaking chills.
distractorExplanations.d: Excess UF causes hypotension and cramps, not fever; shaking chills after connection point to infection.

prompt: A patient arrives 5 kg above target weight, short of breath and unable to lie flat. What should the technician do?

options.text: Lay the patient flat so the fluid redistributes before cannulation
Weigh again after the patient voids and walks for a few minutes
Start treatment with a high UF rate without informing the nurse
Keep them upright, notify the nurse now, and check vital signs

explanation: A large weight gain with shortness of breath and inability to lie flat suggests fluid overload with possible pulmonary edema, a medical emergency. Keep the patient sitting upright, notify the nurse immediately, and obtain vital signs and oxygen saturation; the nurse and provider direct treatment and UF.

distractorExplanations.a: Lying flat worsens breathing in pulmonary edema; patients who cannot lie flat are kept upright.
distractorExplanations.b: Delaying for a reweigh ignores a breathing emergency; the nurse must be told immediately.
distractorExplanations.c: A high UF rate on an unstable patient risks hypotension, and the nurse must direct care in an emergency.

prompt: A patient asks when to take their prescribed phosphate binder. What is the correct teaching point to reinforce?

options.text: Take it at bedtime so it works overnight
Take it with meals and snacks as prescribed
Take it right after each dialysis session
Take it on an empty stomach before breakfast

explanation: Phosphate binders work in the gut by binding phosphorus in food so it is excreted instead of absorbed. They must be taken with meals and snacks as prescribed; taken without food they bind little phosphorus. Detailed diet and drug teaching comes from the dietitian, nurse or provider.

distractorExplanations.a: At bedtime there is no food in the gut to bind, so the binder has almost nothing to act on.
distractorExplanations.c: Dialysis removes some phosphorus, but binders act on food, so timing them to dialysis misses the meals.
distractorExplanations.d: An empty stomach defeats the purpose; binders must be in the gut together with food to bind phosphorus.

prompt: A patient on a fluid restriction says they drink very little water but still gain a lot between treatments. Which hidden fluid source should be discussed?

options.text: Ice chips, soup, gelatin and ice cream count as fluid
Fresh fruit and vegetables contain no fluid to count
Coffee and tea do not count because they cause urination
Plain water is the one drink that counts toward the limit

explanation: Anything liquid at room temperature counts toward fluid intake, including ice, soup, gelatin, ice cream and popsicles, and salty food drives thirst. Pointing out these hidden sources helps patients control interdialytic weight gain; specific limits are set by the care team.

distractorExplanations.b: Many fruits and vegetables are mostly water, and some are high in potassium, so they are not fluid-free.
distractorExplanations.c: Most dialysis patients make little urine, so coffee and tea count fully toward the fluid limit.
distractorExplanations.d: All liquids and foods that melt count toward the limit, not just plain water.

prompt: During treatment the blood in the venous line turns cherry-red and translucent, and the patient reports chest tightness and back pain. What should the technician do?

options.text: Return the blood with saline quickly, then disconnect the patient
Lower the dialysate temperature and continue while watching symptoms
Stop the pump, clamp lines, do not return blood, and call the RN
Increase blood flow to clear damaged cells through the dialyzer faster

explanation: Cherry-red, translucent venous blood with chest or back pain signals acute hemolysis. Returning that blood would give the patient a potassium load from burst red cells, so per protocol the pump is stopped, lines are clamped, blood is not returned, the nurse is called, and the dialysate and water are checked.

distractorExplanations.a: Hemolyzed blood carries a high potassium load; returning it can cause dangerous hyperkalemia, so it is not given back.
distractorExplanations.b: Hemolysis can also come from chloramine or wrong conductivity, so treatment is stopped rather than continued.
distractorExplanations.d: Faster flow keeps exposing blood to the cause; the circuit is stopped and clamped instead.

prompt: A patient with diabetes becomes shaky, sweaty and confused during treatment. What should the technician do?

options.text: Assume intradialytic hypotension and give a saline bolus first
Check blood glucose per protocol and notify the nurse right away
Lower the UF rate and wait for symptoms to settle on their own
Encourage the patient to sleep and recheck at the end of treatment

explanation: Shakiness, sweating and confusion in a patient with diabetes suggest hypoglycemia, which can occur during dialysis, especially with missed meals or low-glucose dialysate. The technician checks glucose per protocol and notifies the nurse so treatment such as oral glucose or IV dextrose can be given.

distractorExplanations.a: Hypotension causes dizziness and yawning; sweating and confusion in a diabetic patient call for a glucose check first.
distractorExplanations.c: Lowering UF does not raise blood glucose, and waiting can let hypoglycemia progress to seizures.
distractorExplanations.d: Confusion is a warning sign, and a hypoglycemic patient left to sleep may lose consciousness.

prompt: During treatment a patient tells the technician they feel hopeless and see no point in continuing dialysis. What is the best response?

options.text: Reassure them that everyone feels this way and change the subject
Tell them stopping dialysis is illegal without a court order
Keep it confidential, since the patient shared it privately
Listen, take it seriously, and tell the nurse or social worker

explanation: Depression is common in dialysis patients and is linked to missed treatments and withdrawal from dialysis. Statements of hopelessness are heard without judgment and reported promptly to the nurse or social worker, who screen for depression and safety; this is not a secret to keep.

distractorExplanations.a: Dismissing the feeling and moving on misses a possible depression or safety risk that the team needs to assess.
distractorExplanations.b: Competent patients may legally choose to stop dialysis; the concern is assessment and support, not legality.
distractorExplanations.c: Hopelessness can signal depression or suicide risk; it must be shared with the care team, not kept secret.

prompt: A facility has two carbon tanks in series. Where is the total chlorine sample drawn before each treatment shift to detect exhaustion early?

options.text: From the RO product water at the distribution loop outlet
From the feed water before the first carbon tank
From the outlet of the second (polisher) carbon tank only
From the port between the worker and polisher tanks

explanation: Testing between the worker and polisher tanks catches chloramine breakthrough while the polisher still protects patients. If the worker result exceeds the limit (commonly cited as 0.1 mg/L total chlorine), the polisher outlet is tested and treatment continues only per protocol, with carbon replaced promptly.

distractorExplanations.a: Testing after RO is too late; RO does not reliably remove chloramine, and carbon exhaustion must be caught upstream.
distractorExplanations.b: Feed water is expected to contain chlorine; the test checks whether carbon is removing it, so it is drawn after carbon.
distractorExplanations.c: Testing only after the polisher means breakthrough is found when no carbon reserve is left to protect patients.

prompt: Water treatment standards specify a minimum empty bed contact time (EBCT) for the carbon system. What does EBCT ensure?

options.text: Water stays in contact with carbon long enough to remove chloramine
The softener has enough time to regenerate between treatment shifts
The RO membrane is flushed long enough after each disinfection
Product water sits in the storage tank long enough to settle particles

explanation: EBCT is the time water spends in contact with the carbon bed, calculated from bed volume and flow rate. Chloramine removal needs adequate contact (standards commonly cite at least 10 minutes total across the carbon tanks), so carbon is sized for peak flow.

distractorExplanations.b: Softener regeneration is controlled by its timer and brine cycle; EBCT is a carbon contact time.
distractorExplanations.c: RO rinsing after disinfection is verified by residual testing, not by an empty bed contact time.
distractorExplanations.d: Storage tanks are discouraged because stagnant water grows bacteria; EBCT refers to the carbon bed.

prompt: RO feed water conductivity is 500 µS/cm and product water conductivity is 25 µS/cm. What is the percent rejection?
explanation: Percent rejection = (feed − product) ÷ feed × 100 = (500 − 25) ÷ 500 × 100 = 475 ÷ 500 × 100 = 95%. Falling rejection signals membrane fouling or damage; the acceptable minimum is set by the manufacturer and facility (often around 90%).

distractorExplanations.a: 5% is the fraction that passes through (25 ÷ 500); rejection is the portion removed, 100% − 5%.
distractorExplanations.b: 90% would mean a product conductivity of 50 µS/cm; here only 25 passes, so rejection is higher.
distractorExplanations.d: 98% would require a product conductivity of 10 µS/cm; 475 ÷ 500 gives 95%.

prompt: Which water treatment component near the start of the system removes suspended particles such as sand and rust?

options.text: A deionizer
The ultraviolet light unit
The polisher carbon tank
The sediment filter

explanation: Multimedia or sediment filters near the start of the pretreatment train trap particles such as sand, silt and rust. Removing them protects the downstream carbon, softener and RO from clogging; the pressure drop across the filter shows when backwashing or replacement is due.

distractorExplanations.a: Deionization removes dissolved ions to make highly pure water; it does not trap sand or rust.
distractorExplanations.b: UV light kills bacteria passing through it; it does not remove particles from the water.
distractorExplanations.c: The polisher carbon tank is a backup for chloramine removal; particles are removed earlier by sediment filtration.

prompt: When should routine water and dialysate culture samples be drawn relative to the scheduled disinfection?

options.text: Right after disinfection, to confirm the system is clean
At any time, since timing has no effect on the result
Only after a patient has a pyrogenic reaction
Just before disinfection, when counts should be highest

explanation: Samples are drawn just before disinfection so they show the system at its worst-case bacterial load. A result within limits at that point means the disinfection interval is adequate; sampling right after disinfection would give falsely reassuring results.

distractorExplanations.a: Sampling right after disinfection captures the cleanest moment and can hide a disinfection interval that is too long.
distractorExplanations.b: Counts climb between disinfections, so timing matters; standards call for worst-case sampling before disinfection.
distractorExplanations.c: Cultures are done on a routine schedule (commonly monthly) to prevent reactions, not only after one occurs.

prompt: After a dialysis machine is disinfected with a chemical such as bleach or peracetic acid, what must be done before the next patient?

options.text: Test for residual disinfectant and confirm a negative result
Run a culture and wait for results before starting treatment
Start the next treatment, since the dialyzer filters out residual
Check only the conductivity, since it detects any disinfectant left

explanation: Chemical disinfectant left in the dialysate path can cross the dialyzer and cause hemolysis or toxic reactions. After rinsing, staff test for residual disinfectant with the method specified for that chemical and document a negative result before the machine is used.

distractorExplanations.b: Cultures take days; they monitor the program but are not a pre-use test after each disinfection.
distractorExplanations.c: The dialyzer membrane does not reliably block disinfectants; residual chemical can reach the blood.
distractorExplanations.d: Conductivity may not detect low residual disinfectant levels; a chemical-specific residual test is required.

prompt: Before modern water treatment, aluminum in dialysis water harmed patients. Which problems was it linked to?

options.text: Pyrogenic reactions and bloodstream infections
Hemolysis and methemoglobinemia
Dialysis encephalopathy and bone disease
Hyperkalemia and cardiac arrhythmias

explanation: Aluminum from feed water or alum-treated city supplies accumulated in dialysis patients, causing dialysis encephalopathy (dementia), aluminum bone disease and anemia. RO and strict limits on aluminum in dialysis water now prevent this, and it is one reason chemical testing continues.

distractorExplanations.a: Pyrogenic reactions and infections come from bacteria and endotoxin, not from dissolved aluminum.
distractorExplanations.b: Hemolysis and methemoglobinemia are typical of chloramine exposure, not aluminum accumulation.
distractorExplanations.d: Hyperkalemia relates to potassium balance; aluminum toxicity affects the brain and the bones.

prompt: When the water distribution loop is designed or modified, why are dead-end branches avoided?

options.text: They lower RO rejection by sending water back to the membrane
They make conductivity readings at the stations inaccurate
They reduce water pressure enough to trigger machine alarms
Stagnant water in them promotes biofilm and bacterial growth

explanation: Dead legs and stagnant segments let water sit still, so bacteria attach and form biofilm that seeds the rest of the loop. Loops are designed for continuous flow without dead ends so that water keeps moving and disinfection reaches every surface.

distractorExplanations.a: Dead legs do not route water back to the RO membrane; their danger is microbial growth from stagnation.
distractorExplanations.b: Station conductivity reflects dialysate mixing, not loop design; stagnation is a microbial problem.
distractorExplanations.c: A small dead leg does not drop loop pressure enough to alarm; it creates a reservoir for bacteria.

prompt: A patient is confirmed HCV antibody-positive. Under CDC guidance for outpatient hemodialysis, how should their treatment be handled?

options.text: Isolate in a separate room with a dedicated machine, as for HBV
Use standard dialysis precautions; isolation is not required
Defer treatment until the viral load is undetectable on testing
Dialyze on the same machine as HBsAg-positive patients

explanation: CDC does not require isolation or dedicated machines for HCV-positive patients; strict adherence to the infection-control practices recommended for all hemodialysis patients prevents spread. Patients are screened for HCV on admission and at intervals set by guidelines, and new infections are investigated.

distractorExplanations.a: Dedicated rooms and machines are CDC recommendations for HBsAg-positive patients; HCV relies on strict standard practices.
distractorExplanations.c: Patients with HCV are not denied dialysis; infection control and referral for antiviral treatment run alongside care.
distractorExplanations.d: HBsAg-positive patients need dedicated machines; placing an HCV patient with them risks HBV infection.

prompt: After a hepatitis B vaccine series, which anti-HBs level is generally considered evidence of immunity?

options.text: At least 1 mIU/mL
At least 10 mIU/mL
At least 100 mIU/mL
At least 1,000 mIU/mL

explanation: An anti-HBs level of 10 mIU/mL or higher after vaccination indicates protection against hepatitis B. Dialysis patients often respond poorly, so they are tested after the series and revaccinated if below 10, and responders are rechecked periodically (CDC recommends annually) with a booster if levels fall.

distractorExplanations.a: Levels below 10 mIU/mL count as a non-response; a level of 1 would trigger revaccination, not show immunity.
distractorExplanations.c: 100 mIU/mL is protective but is not the threshold; 10 mIU/mL is the cutoff used by CDC.
distractorExplanations.d: No level this high is required; any result at or above 10 mIU/mL counts as a vaccine response.

prompt: A patient has just been disconnected and has left the station. What must happen before the next patient is seated there?

options.text: Wipe only visibly soiled areas, since the chair looks clean otherwise
Change the chair cover but leave the machine surfaces for end of day
Clean and disinfect the chair, machine and all station surfaces
Spray disinfectant while the next patient sits and let it air dry

explanation: CDC recommends that after each patient leaves, the chair, machine exterior, control panel, tray table and other station surfaces are cleaned and disinfected with an EPA-registered product for its contact time. Blood contamination is often invisible, so surfaces are treated whether or not they look soiled.

distractorExplanations.a: Blood contamination is often not visible; every station surface is disinfected between patients.
distractorExplanations.b: Machine surfaces are touched constantly and carry blood; they are disinfected between patients, not once a day.
distractorExplanations.d: Disinfecting around a seated patient exposes them to chemicals and does not allow proper cleaning.

prompt: Blood has wetted the external transducer protector on the venous pressure line during treatment. What should be done?

options.text: Wipe the protector with alcohol and keep using it for the session
Flush the line with saline to push the blood back toward the patient
Leave it until the end of treatment, then replace it before the next patient
Replace it, and have the machine-side protector checked per policy

explanation: A wetted transducer protector no longer protects: pressure readings become unreliable and blood may have reached the internal (machine-side) protector, which can carry bloodborne viruses to the next patient. Replace the external protector and have the internal side inspected per policy, often by biomed.

distractorExplanations.a: Alcohol does not restore a wetted filter membrane, and readings stay unreliable; it must be replaced.
distractorExplanations.b: Flushing can push contaminated fluid either way and does not fix the wet protector or the internal contamination risk.
distractorExplanations.c: Waiting leaves pressure monitoring unreliable for the rest of treatment and risks contaminating the machine.

prompt: CDC core interventions for preventing dialysis bloodstream infections recommend which skin antiseptic for catheter exit-site care?

options.text: Povidone-iodine without alcohol as first choice
Hydrogen peroxide to bubble away bacteria
Alcohol-based chlorhexidine (above 0.5%)
Plain 70% alcohol wipes used alone

explanation: CDC's Core Interventions for dialysis bloodstream infection prevention recommend an alcohol-based chlorhexidine (>0.5%) solution for skin antisepsis at catheter exit sites, with povidone-iodine (preferably with alcohol) or 70% alcohol as alternatives when chlorhexidine is contraindicated.

distractorExplanations.a: Povidone-iodine is an alternative when chlorhexidine cannot be used, not the first choice under CDC core interventions.
distractorExplanations.b: Hydrogen peroxide is not recommended for catheter exit-site antisepsis and can damage tissue.
distractorExplanations.d: 70% alcohol alone is listed only as an alternative; it lacks chlorhexidine's lasting antimicrobial activity.

prompt: In a dialyzer reprocessing program, a reused dialyzer's fiber bundle volume is measured before each use. Which result means the dialyzer must be discarded?

options.text: Below 50% of the original volume
Below 80% of the original volume
Below 90% of the original volume
Below 98% of the original volume

explanation: Fiber bundle volume reflects how many fibers are still open; clotted or blocked fibers lower clearance. AAMI reuse standards call for discarding a dialyzer when its volume falls below 80% of the original measurement, as well as after failed pressure tests or visible defects.

distractorExplanations.a: Waiting until half the fibers are blocked would deliver badly inadequate dialysis; the cutoff is 80%.
distractorExplanations.c: 90% is stricter than the standard; dialyzers are discarded when volume falls below 80% of the original.
distractorExplanations.d: Some volume loss is expected with reuse; a 98% cutoff would discard nearly every dialyzer, while the standard is 80%.

prompt: A hardness test on softener outlet water at the end of the day is above the limit. What usually restores the softener?

options.text: Regenerating resin with salt (NaCl) brine
Replacing the carbon in the worker tank
Disinfecting the resin with bleach overnight
Raising the RO feed pressure to compensate

explanation: Softener resin exchanges sodium for calcium and magnesium until its sodium is used up. Regeneration with sodium chloride brine from the salt tank recharges it; end-of-day hardness tests show whether regeneration frequency and the salt supply are adequate.

distractorExplanations.b: Carbon removes chlorine and chloramine; replacing it does not restore hardness removal.
distractorExplanations.c: Bleach disinfects but does not recharge ion-exchange resin, and it can damage the resin.
distractorExplanations.d: Higher RO pressure does not remove hardness and speeds scaling of the membrane.

prompt: Venous needle dislodgement may not trigger a venous pressure alarm. Which practice best protects patients from this risk?

options.text: Cover the access arm with a blanket so the patient stays warm
Set the venous pressure alarm limits wider to reduce false alarms
Check the access when an alarm sounds during treatment
Secure needles and lines, and keep the access site in view

explanation: If a venous needle slips out, blood is pumped onto the bed while venous pressure may drop only slightly, so alarms are not reliable. Securing needles and lines per protocol, keeping the access uncovered and visible, and checking it at every monitoring round let blood loss be caught within seconds.

distractorExplanations.a: A blanket over the access hides needle dislodgement and bleeding; the site must remain visible.
distractorExplanations.b: Wider limits make the alarm even less likely to catch the small pressure drop from dislodgement.
distractorExplanations.c: Dislodgement often does not alarm, so waiting for an alarm can allow major blood loss.

prompt: A technician notices they recorded the wrong post weight on a paper flowsheet. How should the error be corrected?

options.text: Use correction fluid and write the right value over it
Draw one line, write the correct value, and initial/date
Scribble out the entry completely so it cannot be misread
Tear out the page and recopy the flowsheet without the error

explanation: Medical records are legal documents, so errors are corrected without hiding the original: one line through the entry so it stays readable, the correct value, and the corrector's initials and date (plus a reason if policy requires). Electronic records use the system's correction or addendum function.

distractorExplanations.a: Correction fluid hides the original entry and makes the record look altered, which undermines its legal value.
distractorExplanations.c: Obliterating the entry looks like concealment; the original must remain readable.
distractorExplanations.d: Destroying and recopying a page amounts to falsifying the record; corrections are made on the original.

prompt: A technician realizes the patient was dialyzed with the wrong dialyzer size for the whole session. The patient feels fine. What should the technician do?

options.text: Tell the nurse now and complete an incident report per policy
Note it only if the patient's labs come back abnormal later
Correct it at the next treatment without reporting the error
Ask a coworker to change the record to show the right dialyzer

explanation: Treatment errors are reported to the nurse promptly and documented through the incident or occurrence system, even when the patient seems unharmed. The nurse and provider assess effects such as reduced clearance, and QAPI uses these reports to fix system causes rather than to blame individuals.

distractorExplanations.b: Waiting for lab results delays assessment, and errors are reported whether or not harm shows up.
distractorExplanations.c: Silently correcting it hides an error the nurse needs to evaluate and that QAPI needs to prevent.
distractorExplanations.d: Changing the record to hide an error is falsification and can cost a technician their certification and job.

prompt: Before starting treatment, how should a technician confirm they have the right patient and prescription?

options.text: Check the chair number on the schedule against the flowsheet
Ask “Are you Mr. Smith?” and wait for the patient to agree
Rely on recognizing the patient from previous treatments
Use two identifiers, such as full name and date of birth

explanation: Patient identification uses at least two identifiers, such as full name and date of birth, checked against the prescription and records. Chair numbers, familiarity and yes/no questions fail when patients swap seats, look alike or are confused, which can lead to the wrong prescription or dialyzer.

distractorExplanations.a: Chair assignments change and patients move; a location is not a patient identifier.
distractorExplanations.b: A yes/no question invites a confused or hard-of-hearing patient to agree; ask them to state their name and birth date.
distractorExplanations.c: Familiarity fails with similar-looking patients or new staff; two identifiers are required every time.

prompt: Power fails during treatment, the machine has no battery backup, and the blood pump stops. What should the technician generally do?

options.text: Disconnect immediately without returning blood to save time
Check the patient and hand-crank the pump per protocol
Leave the patient connected and wait for power to return
Open the venous clamp so blood drains back by gravity

explanation: When the machine loses power, the blood pump stops and the circuit can clot. Per protocol and the manufacturer's instructions, the technician checks the patient and uses the manual hand crank to keep blood moving or return it with saline, watching for air by eye because the air detector may not work without power.

distractorExplanations.a: Disconnecting without returning blood discards the circuit's blood volume; manual rinseback is done when it is safe.
distractorExplanations.c: Waiting with the pump stopped lets the circuit clot and leaves the patient unmonitored.
distractorExplanations.d: Opening the clamp without the pump and air detector risks air entry and uncontrolled flow.

prompt: Which practice is correct for disposing of fistula needles after treatment?

options.text: Recap the needles with two hands before carrying them to the bin
Place them in the regular trash inside a closed plastic bag
Drop them into a puncture-resistant sharps container at once
Fill the sharps container to the top before replacing it

explanation: OSHA requires used sharps to go immediately into a closable, puncture-resistant, leak-proof, labeled sharps container placed close to the point of use. Two-handed recapping causes needle-sticks, and containers are replaced at the fill line rather than overfilled.

distractorExplanations.a: Two-handed recapping is a leading cause of needle-sticks; OSHA prohibits it except by approved one-handed methods.
distractorExplanations.b: Plastic bags tear and expose staff to needle-sticks; sharps go into puncture-resistant containers.
distractorExplanations.d: Overfilled containers cause needle-sticks; they are closed and replaced when they reach the fill line.

prompt: Acid concentrate splashes into a technician's eyes while changing a jug. What is the correct first action?

options.text: Rinse briefly with saline from a syringe and return to work
Rub the eyes with a clean towel and then call the supervisor
Apply a neutralizing bicarbonate solution to the eyes
Flush at the eyewash station continuously for 15 minutes

explanation: Chemical eye splashes need immediate, continuous flushing at an eyewash station (the ANSI eyewash standard calls for 15 minutes) while holding the eyelids open, then reporting the exposure and getting medical evaluation. The SDS for the concentrate lists specific first-aid steps.

distractorExplanations.a: A brief syringe rinse does not remove enough chemical; continuous flushing for about 15 minutes is needed.
distractorExplanations.b: Rubbing spreads the chemical and can scratch the cornea; flush first, then report the exposure.
distractorExplanations.c: Neutralizing agents in the eye can cause a heat-producing reaction and more injury; flush with water instead.

prompt: A technician plans to run a bleach disinfection right after an acid (citric or acetic) cleaning cycle on the same equipment. Why must the system be rinsed between them?

options.text: Bleach left with acid forms scale that clogs the RO membrane
Acid neutralizes bleach completely, so the disinfection fails
Mixing bleach with any acid can release toxic chlorine gas
Acid raises the conductivity, so the machine will not start

explanation: Sodium hypochlorite (bleach) reacts with acids to release chlorine gas, which can injure staff and patients. Chemicals are never mixed, cycles are separated by thorough rinsing per the manufacturer, and the SDS and facility procedures are followed for every disinfectant.

distractorExplanations.a: The danger is not scale; it is the toxic gas released when bleach meets acid.
distractorExplanations.b: Acid does change bleach chemistry, but the key hazard is chlorine gas release, not just weaker disinfection.
distractorExplanations.d: Conductivity alarms are a dialysate issue; the reason to rinse between bleach and acid is gas release.

prompt: Which federal rules set the minimum health and safety requirements that Medicare-certified US dialysis facilities must meet?

options.text: OSHA's Hazard Communication Standard
HIPAA Privacy and Security Rules
FDA medical device clearance rules
CMS ESRD Conditions for Coverage

explanation: The CMS End-Stage Renal Disease Conditions for Coverage (42 CFR Part 494) are the federal requirements for Medicare-certified dialysis facilities, covering water quality, infection control, patient rights, QAPI and staff qualifications. State surveyors inspect facilities against them.

distractorExplanations.a: OSHA HazCom covers chemical hazards for workers; it does not set the overall care and safety requirements for dialysis facilities.
distractorExplanations.b: HIPAA governs the privacy of health information; it does not set dialysis care and safety standards.
distractorExplanations.c: FDA clears dialysis machines and devices but does not certify how dialysis facilities operate.

prompt: Under federal Medicare rules for dialysis facilities, within what period after hire must a patient care dialysis technician become certified under a state or national program?

options.text: 6 months
12 months
18 months
24 months

explanation: The CMS ESRD Conditions for Coverage require patient care dialysis technicians to complete a training program and to be certified under a state or nationally recognized program (such as NNCC's CCHT) within 18 months of being hired as a technician. Some states add their own requirements.

distractorExplanations.a: Six months is shorter than the federal rule; CMS allows 18 months from hire to become certified.
distractorExplanations.b: 12 months is not the CMS deadline; technicians have 18 months after hire to certify.
distractorExplanations.d: 24 months exceeds the CMS limit; certification must be obtained within 18 months of hire.

prompt: A patient complains to the technician about how they were treated by staff. What should the technician do?

options.text: Tell the patient complaints can be made only to the state
Defend the coworker and explain why the patient is wrong
Ignore it, since grievances are handled by the administrator
Listen, tell the nurse, and explain the grievance steps

explanation: Patients have the right to voice grievances without retaliation, through the facility's internal process or externally to the state survey agency or ESRD Network. The technician listens respectfully, informs the nurse or manager, and makes sure the patient knows how to file a grievance.

distractorExplanations.a: Patients may use the facility process or outside routes; saying only the state can help blocks their rights.
distractorExplanations.b: Arguing dismisses the complaint and can feel like retaliation, which patient-rights rules prohibit.
distractorExplanations.c: Ignoring a complaint fails the patient; staff pass it on so the grievance process can work.

prompt: A long-term patient offers the technician cash as a thank-you and asks to connect on social media. What is the appropriate response?

options.text: Accept the cash if it is under the facility's gift limit
Politely decline both, per facility boundary policy
Accept the social media request but decline the money
Accept both, since refusing could harm the relationship

explanation: Professional boundaries keep the relationship focused on the patient's care. Most facilities prohibit accepting cash and connecting with patients on personal social media, which also risks privacy breaches; the technician declines kindly, follows facility policy, and asks a supervisor if unsure.

distractorExplanations.a: Cash gifts are generally prohibited regardless of amount; any gift allowance in policy covers small non-cash items.
distractorExplanations.c: Personal social media connections blur boundaries and risk exposing protected health information.
distractorExplanations.d: Accepting cash and social contact crosses professional boundaries, even if declining feels awkward.

prompt: A technician needs to report a patient's falling blood pressure to the nurse. Which communication format organizes the report clearly?

options.text: SBAR: situation, background, assessment, recommendation
SOAP: subjective, objective, assessment, plan
PRN: as needed, whenever the nurse has free time to listen
RACE: rescue, alarm, contain, extinguish

explanation: SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) is a structured format for urgent clinical handoffs that gives the nurse the key facts quickly: what is happening, relevant history, what the technician observed, and what is needed. Many dialysis units train technicians to use it.

distractorExplanations.b: SOAP is a charting format for provider notes, not a quick verbal report of an urgent change.
distractorExplanations.c: PRN means as needed for medication timing; a falling blood pressure is reported now, not when convenient.
distractorExplanations.d: RACE is the fire response sequence, not a format for reporting a patient's condition.

prompt: How should gauze and tubing saturated with blood be discarded at the end of treatment?

options.text: In regular trash, since dried blood is no longer infectious
In a labeled red biohazard bag for regulated medical waste
In the sharps container along with the used needles
In the recycling bin after rinsing the tubing with water

explanation: Items saturated or caked with blood are regulated medical waste under OSHA and state rules and go into labeled red biohazard bags or containers. Sharps go only in sharps containers, and lightly soiled items may go in regular trash depending on state definitions.

distractorExplanations.a: Dried blood can still carry hepatitis B virus; saturated items are regulated medical waste.
distractorExplanations.c: Sharps containers are for needles and other sharp items; bulky soft waste belongs in biohazard bags.
distractorExplanations.d: Blood-contaminated tubing is not recycled; rinsing exposes staff and does not decontaminate it.

prompt: As part of emergency preparedness, what do dialysis patients learn to do if a disaster prevents treatment for several days?

options.text: Increase fluids to dilute toxins until dialysis is available
Eat normally, since a few missed days have little effect
Go to any hospital and expect same-day dialysis there
Follow a strict emergency diet low in fluid and potassium

explanation: CMS requires dialysis facilities to have emergency preparedness plans and to teach patients what to do when treatment is disrupted. A stricter emergency diet limiting fluid, potassium, sodium and protein slows the buildup of fluid and potassium until dialysis resumes at an alternate site.

distractorExplanations.a: Extra fluid cannot be removed without dialysis and risks pulmonary edema.
distractorExplanations.b: Fluid and potassium build up quickly; a few missed days can be life-threatening without diet changes.
distractorExplanations.c: Hospitals may be overwhelmed in a disaster; patients follow the facility plan and the emergency diet meanwhile.
